newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Profits surge at UK publisher Dorling.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Profits surge at UK publisher Dorling.

text.p: British publisher Dorling Kindersley extended its strong growth record when it announced on Monday that annual profit had risen by more than a third.

Pre-tax profit for the year to June 30 totalled 17.4 million pounds ($27 million), a rise of 37 percent on the 1995 level of 12.7 million pounds. The total dividend was increased to 4.5 pence per share from 3.9p.

Commenting on the results, chairman and chief executive Peter Kindersley said they "centred around the high quality of the DK product and the fact that we are world based, not dependent on one market".
A publisher of illustrated reference books and CD-ROMS, Dorling has long been a darling of British share analysts who cite its growth potential in the multi-media age.
Dorling shares had added 13.5p to 545p by 1325 GMT on Monday. The company was floated on the London Stock Exchange in 1992 at a price of 165p.

U.S. software giant Microsoft sold out of the company last November, disposing of a 17.9 percent stake at a price of 507p a share. Microsoft had first taken a substantial holding in the company four years earlier.
Turnover in the year increased by 25 percent to 174 million pounds, 77 percent of which came from overseas. U.S. turnover has doubled in the past two years and totalled 66.6 million pounds last year.
Formed in 1974 by Peter Kindersley and the now retired Christopher Dorling, the London-based company has expanded into the multimedia market with a number of successful CD-ROM titles.
Its multimedia division increased its turnover by 62 percent to 21.2 million pounds in the past year.
Company executives said that the division should continue to expand in the current year despite problems of overcrowding in the U.S. retail market.
"Multimedia, particularly in the U.S., is very tough this year and we recognise that," Kindersley told a press conference.
"People have become too competitive, they are trying to create a mass market for something which is not a mass market product," he added.
But he added that a stable market for CD-ROMs should emerge once the shake-up in the U.S. was complete.
